dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'edh' naturally takes Atmanepada endings because it is marked with an anudatta accent (anudattet), meaning the state of growing or prospering belongs to the subject. When you make someone else grow or cultivate something, a causative suffix (Nic) is added, turning it into 'edhayati'.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'edha' is taught in the sense of 'vriddhi' (growth or accumulation). It is anudattet and therefore strictly takes Atmanepada terminations. As an ardhadhatuka set root, it receives the intermediate augment 'it' in non-sarvadhatuka forms (e.g., edhita, edhishyate). Lit forms take the am-pratyaya (edhamchakre).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'edha vriddhau' as anudattet and atmanepadi. Vriddhi signifies upachaya (physical or metaphorical expansion). Forms include edhate (Lat), edhamchakre (Lit), edhita (Lut), and edhishyate (Lrt).

meanings.English: to grow, to prosper, to increase, to flourish

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'spardh' means to compete, rival, or vie with someone. Because it belongs to the Atmanepada group, it always uses endings like -te, -ete, -nte in the active present tense. When we want to say 'to make someone compete', we add the causative marker -i- (Nic), which changes the pada to Parasmaipada.

meanings.English: to compete, to rival, to vie with, to challenge

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhu' signifies 'to be', 'to exist', or 'to become'. In standard active voice (kartari prayoga), it takes Parasmaipada endings to express an ongoing state of existence (bhavati). When modified by the causative affix (nic), it takes the sense of 'causing to be', 'producing', or 'cherishing' (bhavayati). In impersonal passive construction (bhave prayoga), it appears with Atmanepada endings as 'bhuyate'.

scenarios.example_english: Truth alone triumphs and remains free from sorrow.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'bhu' is placed at the very head of the Dhatupatha in the sense of 'satta' (existence, being). Being udatta and lacking markers for Atmanepada, it universally takes Parasmaipada affixes in standard kartari usage. The penultimate/final u-kara undergoes guna ('o') followed by av-adesha before sarvadhatuka affixes, generating the base 'bhava-'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin highlights that 'bhu' serves as the auspicious opening (mangalartha) of the entire verbal lexicon. The condition of satta denotes pure reality or becoming. In causal formations, through vriddhi and nic-pratyaya, it conveys manifesting or bringing an object into existence (utpadana).

meanings.English: To be, to exist, to become

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'badh' (badhri/badhate) means to trouble, torment, annoy, or harass. Because it is inherently Atmanepada, it uses terminations like -te (badhate). In simple sentences, it expresses someone facing distress or pain caused by heat, enemies, or illness.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active voice), Present Tense (Lat Lakara), 3rd Person Singular (Prathama Purusha Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The summer heat afflicts the traveler.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root badhri (badhate) is classified in the Bhvadi Gana under the meaning 'lodanam' (to harass, perturb, or agitate). It is an Atmanepadi, Set root ending with the anubandha 'ri', indicating standard formation of forms in sarvadhatuka and ardhadhatuka tenses without irregular vowel loss.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'badhri lodane' as the act of troubling, agitating, or causing impediment (upaghata). It yields the primary present form 'badhate' and expresses transitive harassment or affliction of an object.

meanings.English: to torment, harass, afflict, or trouble
meanings.Bengali: kashto deya, piran kora, jontrona deya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gadh' means to stand firmly (gain reputation), to eagerly desire something, or to weave/compose together. It is an Atmanepada verb, meaning the action reflects an internal orientation or personal engagement of the subject.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wise person seeks what is good.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic (Causative), Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to establish or string together

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'gadhṛ' belongs to the Bhvadi gana and carries the anubandha 'ṛ'. It functions in three primary semantic domains: pratishtha (establishment or firm standing), lipsa (intense desire to acquire), and grantha (intertwining or composing). Being an Atmanepadi root, it yields forms like gadhate in the present tense and jagadhe in the perfect tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin elucidates that the marker 'ṛ' serves specific derivational rules in the secondary conjugation. The three distinct spheres of meaning denote achieving prestige, longing for an object, and stringing units into an organized whole.

meanings.English: To establish oneself, to desire eagerly to obtain, to string together or weave

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nadh' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is conjugated in the Atmanepada. It conveys four main meanings: begging/requesting (yanca), suffering or torment (upatapa), supreme power/lordship (aishvarya), and blessing or well-wishing (ashis). In simple everyday usage, it functions similarly to 'yac' when asking for something, or expresses experiencing distress.

scenarios.meaning: You all seek or pray for blessings

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'nadhri' is anudattetta and takes Atmanepada terminations. It signifies yanca (solicitation/petition), upatapa (affliction/torment), aishvarya (mastery/sovereignty), and ashis (benediction). Morphologically, it forms 'nadhate' with shab-pratyaya.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'nadhri' parallels 'nadhri' with a short vowel base. Its semantics span requesting, experiencing pain, ruling, and blessing. The root is treated as set in standard conjugation.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dadh' expresses the action of holding, wearing, or sustaining. Because it belongs to the Atmanepada group in the Bhvadi class, the action is conceived as reflecting upon or directly concerning the subject. Adding the causative suffix (nic) extends the meaning to causing someone to wear or hold something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana, Lat Lakara (Present Tense), Prathama Purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (Singular), Atmanepada

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dadha' (read also as 'dadhi' in certain recensions) is listed in the Bhvadi gana with the semantic indicator 'dharane' (holding/bearing). It takes Atmanepada affixes by general rule and is anit/set according to anubandha analysis, conjugating as dadhate, dadhate, dadhante in the present tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses the root in the sense of 'dharanam' (supporting, wearing, or holding up). He notes the regular application of shap vikarana yielding standard Bhvadi middle-voice derivations.

meanings.English: to hold, to wear, to bear, to sustain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root skund means to jump, leap, or move haltingly. Because it has an indicatory 'i' (idit), an internal nasal 'n' is added, giving the base 'skunda-'. It takes Atmanepada endings in standard active voice. When used with causative suffixes (nic), it means to cause someone or something to leap or bounce.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śvind' means to become white, whiten, or shine brightly with whiteness. Because it is marked as anudāttet, it takes Ātmanepada endings in the active sense. In the causative form (Nic), it changes meaning from 'becoming white' to 'making something white' (bleaching or painting white).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root śvidi has the it-marker 'i' (idit), which causes the insertion of a penultimate nasal (num-agama), yielding the base form śvind-. It denotes śvaitya (the state of being white or whitening). By being anudāttopadeśa, it takes Ātmanepada pratyayas in kartari prayoga: śvindate, śaśvinde, śvinditā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes śvidi śvaitye as an idit root denoting whiteness or attaining whiteness. Due to idit-tva, the nasal is retained throughout non-lopa environments, forming present forms like śvindate and perfect forms like śaśvinde.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root vand means to salute respectfully, to bow down, or to praise. It inherently takes Atmanepada endings (e.g., vandate). When used in causative forms, it conveys making or guiding someone else to offer respect or homage.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root vadi~ is idit, which mandates the insertion of num-agama by the rule idito num dhatoh, resulting in the base vand. It is anudatta-it, hence it takes Atmanepada affixes. The primary meanings are abhivadana (reverential bowing/salutation) and stuti (praise).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that because of the idit marker, nasal augmentation (num) occurs, yielding vandate. He glosses abhivadanam as pranamah (reverential prostration) and stutih as gunavarnanam (extolling virtues).

meanings.English: to salute, to praise, to pay homage

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'nath' generally means to ask, beg, suffer distress, rule, or give blessings. Because it has an 'r' marker in its original grammatical form (nathri), it generally takes Atmanepada endings ('nathate'). However, in classical usage, when expressing a blessing (asirvacana) without an object, it can take Parasmaipada forms ('nathati') per specific Paninian rules.

The 'r' it-marker denotes Atmanepada by default, though special sutras apply for pada alternation in blessing senses.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'nathri' functions in the senses of prayer, requesting, suffering, and commanding. When used in the sense of giving a benediction (asirarthe), genitive case syntax and Parasmaipada variants are traditionally discussed with reference to Ashtadhyayi rules.

When used with causative affixes (ṇic), it shifts to meaning making someone else angry.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root katth means to praise, boast, or speak highly of someone or oneself. It takes Atmanepada endings by default. When used normally, it denotes boasting or praising. In its causative form (katthayati), it signifies causing someone else to praise or boast.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root kattha is placed under the Bhvadi class with the meaning shlagha (praise or self-glorification). It is anudattopadesha, hence inherently taking Atmanepada affixes. Forms generated include katthate in present tense, cakatthe in perfect tense (lit), and katthita in periphrastic future (lut).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin states kattha shlaghayam to signify vocal praise or bragging. It is marked as set and atmanepadi. Nominal derivatives such as katthana (the act of boasting or praising) are regularly formed.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cah' means to cheat, deceive, harass, or act hypocritically. It inherently takes Atmanepada endings in the present tense (cahate). When converted into a causative (nic) form, it expresses making someone deceive or harass another.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya explains 'caha parikalkane' where parikalkana denotes deception, hypocrisy (dambha), or causing affliction (peedana). Being anudatta-it, the root takes Atmanepada affixes (cahate, cehe, cahita, cahishyate).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin identifies 'kalkanam' as 'dambhah khedanam va' (fraudulence, pretension, or distressing others). It forms regular Bhvadi grade forms with intermediate -i- (it) in non-sarvadhatuka environments where applicable.

meanings.English: to deceive, cheat, harass, or act hypocritically

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root klis means to experience distress, pain, or suffering. vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes klis in the sense of affliction or suffering (upatapa). As an anudatta-it root in this class, it is conjugated in the Atmanepada, producing roots that represent enduring pain.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kshij' refers to making an inarticulate, indistinct sound such as murmuring, creaking, buzzing, or groaning. vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kshiji' belongs to the Bhvadi class and is read with anudatta accentuation, establishing its Atmanepada character. vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'kshiji' under the sense of unexpressed sound (avyakta-dhvani). The guna modification of the vowel 'i' to 'e' occurs before sarvadhatuka affixes, yielding 'ksejate'. It is strictly akarmaka (intransitive) in its primary sense.

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kas' means to shine, appear radiant, or be visible. Because it takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form, it describes the subject naturally exhibiting brightness. With causative markers, it changes to illuminating or displaying something.

vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini treats 'kasri diptau' as an intransitive root denoting luminosity and brilliance. The commentary highlights the morphological marker 'ri' and illustrates basic finite formations including kasate, cakase, and kasita.

meanings.English: To shine, to gleam, to be visible or radiant

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhāṣ' means to articulate speech or to speak clearly. When made into a causative (making someone else speak), it can take standard causative forms like bhāṣayati.

scenarios.example_english: The moon shines in the sky.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative active)
scenarios.example_english: The lamp illuminates the house.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhashri with anubandha ri is glossed under diptau, signifying brightness, radiance, or illumination. The indicative marker ri denotes specific grammatical operations in the aorist, taking Atmanepada affixes in the basic system.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes bhashri in the opening section of the Bhvadi-gana among verbs of shining and luminescence, noting its regular Atmanepada paradigm (bhashate, bhashante) and akarmaka (intransitive) syntax.

meanings.English: to shine, to be bright, to illuminate

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verbal root 'rash' means to make a sound, utter a cry, or howl. Being strictly Atmanepada in its primary conjugation, it takes endings like -te, -ete, -nte to describe a subject producing vocal sounds or animal noises. When made causative with the -nic affix, it means to cause someone or something to emit a sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Lat lakara (Present Indicative), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana, Atmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The animal makes a sound in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to cry or make noise
scenarios.example_english: The herdsman causes the beast to make a sound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: rashri shabde - 'rashate'. Anudatta-ittvena atmanepadi. Rkarasya it-samjna tu bharadvajiyenisthadi-vikalpa-vidhanartha bhavati. Reshe, rashita, rashishyate ityadi rupani sidhyanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: rashri shabde - rashate. Shabdo dhvananam uccharanam va. Rkaro 'nudattarthah. Reshe, rashita, arashita.

meanings.English: to make a sound, to howl, to cry out
meanings.German: einen Laut von sich geben, heulen, schreien
meanings.Chinese: fachu shengyin, hao jiao, ming jiao

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śaś' means to leap, spring, or jump, which is the source of the Sanskrit word 'śaśa' (hare or rabbit). In basic usage, it takes standard Parasmaipada endings to describe an animal or person bounding or jumping forward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra (Present Active 3rd Person Singular)
scenarios.example_english: The hare leaps in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Ṇijanta (Causative), Laṭ lakāra
scenarios.example_english: The hunter causes the deer to leap.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: śaśṛ plutagatau. ṛkāro aṅ-artham. plutaṁ nāma plavamānaṁ gamanam. śaśati, śaśataḥ, śaśanti. aśiśat.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: śaśṛ plutagatau. plutaṁ plavanam. śaśatīti. asmād eva śaśaḥ śaśakaḥ.

meanings.English: to leap, to jump, to bound

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root hlad means to experience joy, refreshment, or happiness. In its simple form, it is used in the Atmanepada (hladate) because the feeling of joy or relief is experienced within oneself. When we want to say someone makes another person happy or delighted, we add the causative suffix nic to make it Parasmaipada (hladayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The child feels delighted with the toy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes joy, gladdens, or refreshes someone
scenarios.example_english: The cool breeze delights everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'hlada sukhe' belongs to the Bhvadi gana. It is marked as anudanvet and therefore takes Atmanepada endings. Being set, the augment it is applied before ardhadhatuka affixes beginning with val (valadi). The primary meaning is sukha-anubhava (experience of happiness or contentment).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'sukhe' as harsha, pritih, or ahlada (gladness, delight). The root follows standard set bhvadi conjugation patterns yielding forms like hladate, jahlade, and hladita.

meanings.English: to be delighted, to be refreshed, to feel happy
meanings.French: se rejouir, etre comble de joie

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mrakṣ' expresses the action of assembling, gathering together, heaping up, or blending. In active voice (Parasmaipada), it shows a subject collecting or packing things together. When combined with the causative suffix, it denotes causing someone to collect or smear/accumulate items.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer gathers the grain together.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/she causes to collect or rub together
scenarios.example_english: The master causes the servant to collect the leaves.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'mrakṣa' is classified under Bhvādi with the meaning 'saṃghāte' (combination, aggregation, or packing together). Being an a-kāravān udātta root without anubandha indicating ātmanepada, it is Parasmaipadi and Seṭ. The primary forms derived include mrakṣati, mamrākṣa / mamrakṣatuḥ, mrakṣitā, and amrakṣīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'mrakṣa saṃghāte' as saṃhatikaraṇa (uniting, compacting, or assembling together into a single whole). He notes the preservation of the kṣ conjunct and the addition of standard Seṭ intermediate i-kāra in ardhadhātuka affixes.

meanings.English: to collect, to heap together, to combine, to smear
meanings.Bengali: ekatrita karā, juro karā, rāśīkṛta karā

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root svad means to taste, savor, relish, or to be delicious. As an Atmanepada verb, it highlights the subject directly experiencing the enjoyment of flavor or a dish being pleasant to taste. When used with causative affixes, it means to make food delicious or to sweeten.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The child relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (causative)
scenarios.example_english: The mother makes the sweet porridge delicious with ghee.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root svada belongs to the Bhvadi class and has the anudatta marker on the vowel, which makes it exclusively Atmanepadi. It is classified as set and denotes asvadana (relishing, tasting, or imparting sweetness and flavor).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes svada asvadane as the root for experiencing taste (rasanubhuti) and palatability. It forms primary derivatives such as svadu (sweet/tasty) and verbal participles like svadita.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to savor, to sweeten, to be pleasant

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prath' means to become famous, to spread out, or to make something well known. Because it is inherently an Atmanepada verb, it takes middle endings like '-te' and '-nte' in the active voice. When used with a causative affix (nic), it changes to mean 'to publish', 'to proclaim', or 'to cause to be famous'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Active voice, Present tense, 3rd person singular, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The fame of the virtuous person spreads across the world.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative, Present tense, 3rd person singular, Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada)
scenarios.example_english: The poet spreads (proclaims) his work everywhere.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti explains 'pratha prakhyane' as spreading, unfolding, or becoming celebrated (prasiddhi). Being an anudattet root, it is classified strictly under Atmanepada in standard usage. The forms in primary tenses include prathate, paprathe, prathishyate, and aprathishta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'prakhyanam' signifies expanding, widening, or attaining renown ('prasiddhih vistaro va'). He lists cognates and standard derivational forms showing the set-nature of the root, maintaining its regular Guna and It-agama behaviors.

meanings.English: to spread, to become famous, to unfold, to proclaim
meanings.Bengali: prasiddha haoya, bistrito haoya, pracharita haoya

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'prasada' denotes the action of spreading out, extending, or diffusing. Because it is an Atmanepada verb, its standard active form takes Atmanepada endings like 'te' (prasadate). When made causative (Nic), it conveys making something spread or dispersing outward.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The fragrance spreads in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the sweet fragrance to spread everywhere.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: prasada visarane. visaranaṃ prasaranam vyaptirva. anudattetvadanudanah atmanepadi. prasadate, prasannata.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: prasada visarane. visaranam viksepah prasaranam va. prasadate, paprasade.

meanings.English: to spread, to diffuse, to expand

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'ślath' means to become loose, untied, or to loosen something. In the basic present tense (lat-lakara), it uses standard Parasmaipada endings like 'ślathati' (it loosens or becomes loose). When used with a causative suffix (nic), it forms 'ślathayati' to describe someone actively loosening or untying an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (active voice), simple present tense (lat-lakara)
scenarios.example_english: The knot becomes loose quickly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative voice), lat-lakara
scenarios.example_english: The boy loosens the rope.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'ślatha' is listed under the Bhvadi class in the sense of making loose or slackening ('śithilīkaraṇe'). It follows the standard thematic conjugation taking 'śap' (a-vikarana) and takes standard Parasmaipada terminations, giving forms like ślathati, śaślatha, ślathitā, and aślathīt.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'ślatha śithilīkaraṇe' as an action indicating the removal of tightness or tension, yielding the primary active stem 'ślatha-'.

meanings.English: to loosen, to slacken, to untie, to become relaxed

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kvanth' means to grieve, lament, or feel sorrow. In the basic active form (Parasmaipada), it describes an individual undergoing deep grief or mourning.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple active voice (Lat, Kartari Prayoga, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The mother grieves due to the sorrow of losing her son.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative form (Nich-pratyaya, Lat, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to grieve or torments with sorrow
scenarios.example_english: The demon's words cause everyone to grieve.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kvantha' is classified in the Bhvadi class with the semantic value 'shoke' (grief, distress). Being an anidit root with dental ending, it retains the th-sound across standard conjugations, forming 'kvanthati' in the present indicative and 'cakvantha' in the perfect.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin lists 'kvantha shoke' among the standard Bhvadi roots denoting an emotional condition of deep suffering or mourning, giving regular forms such as kvanthati, cakvantha, and kvanthita.

meanings.English: to grieve, to lament, to suffer distress or sorrow

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'granth' means to string together, arrange, compose, or weave elements systematically. In simple present active voice (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent stringing flowers, assembling words, or composing a book. When used with the causative affix (Nich), it denotes causing someone else to compose or arrange things.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The poet composes a book.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: Causes to compose / gets strung together
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student compose a treatise.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'grantha sandarbhe' belongs to the Bhvadi class. 'Sandarbha' signifies methodical arrangement, tying together, or structural composition (such as literary creation or stringing a garland). Being marked as anudattopadesha-free with dental endings, it takes the standard 'it' augment in non-sarvadhatuka forms and forms 'granthati'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'grantha' has the semantic sense of 'sandarbha' (composition or connection). It denotes linking parts into an integrated whole, such as words into a sentence or flowers into a garland. The primary derivation gives 'granthanam' and 'grantha'.

meanings.English: to string together, to compose, to arrange, to bind
meanings.Hindi: rachana karna, guthana, piro na, bandhana
meanings.Chinese: bian zhi, zhuan xie, lian jie

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'arth' means to ask, request, or beg for something. It is used in the Atmanepada form (arthayate) because the result of the request directly benefits the agent. When you want to ask someone for help, knowledge, or an object, this root is used.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat-lakara (present tense, singular)
scenarios.example_english: The student requests knowledge from the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat-lakara (present tense, plural)
scenarios.example_english: The beggars ask the king for wealth.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'artha' is listed in the sense of 'yacana' (requesting, begging). It is an Atmanepadi root taking the customary affixes to form arthayate. Because of its semantic import of praying or supplicating, it governs two objects (dvitiya) according to 'akathitam ca' when applicable, functioning transitively.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'artha yacayam' as being Atmanepada. It denotes the act of seeking or soliciting. Derivative nominals like 'arthin' (seeker/supplicant) and 'prarthana' (prayer/request with prefix pra) originate directly from this semantic base.

meanings.English: to ask, to request, to beg, to desire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'śard' means to discharge, emit, or break wind. It is an Atmanepada verb where the primary form 'śardate' describes the act of bodily release or expulsion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra (present tense, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The patient expels downward gas.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇijanta (causative), kartari prayoga, laṭ lakāra
scenarios.example_english: The medicine causes the bodily impurity to be expelled.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: śardi utsarge. utsargaḥ apānavāyoh tyāgaḥ. ātmanepadī seṭ. śardate, śardāñcakre, śarditā.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: śardi utsarge. utsargo visargaḥ apānavāyvādestyāgaḥ. śardate, śardiṣyate.

meanings.English: to discharge, to emit, to break wind

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gard' means to make a harsh, bad, or unpleasant sound (such as grunting, groaning, or braying). As an inherently Atmanepada verb, it takes middle endings (gardate). When used in the causative (Nic), it means to cause someone or something to make an unpleasant sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: makes a harsh or unpleasant sound / brays
scenarios.example_english: The donkey brays loudly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to emit a harsh or unpleasant sound
scenarios.example_english: The warrior causes the enemy to groan in distress with a strike.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'gardi kutsitashabde' as an anudatteta Atmanepadi root belonging to the Bhvadi gana. It denotes making an inauspicious, defective, or reproachable vocal sound.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin glosses 'gardi' under the sense of producing a defective or contemptible auditory noise (kutsita-dhvani), highlighting its primary use in expressing unpleasant animal vocalizations or crude shouting.

meanings.English: to make an unpleasant sound, to bray, to groan
meanings.Malayalam: asukhadakaramaya shabdham undakku, kazhutha pole karayu
meanings.Hindi: ashubha ya ashravya shabda karna, gardabh ke saman bolna
meanings.Bengali: katu ba kutsita shabda kara, gadhar mata daka
meanings.German: ein unangenehmes Geraeusch machen, schreien, roehren
meanings.French: emettre un son desagreable, braire, grogner

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'krund' comes from the aupadeshika form 'krudi~' and means 'to sink', 'to plunge', or 'to immerse oneself into water'. The letter 'i' at the end is an 'it' marker (idit), which causes a nasal sound 'n' to be inserted into the middle of the root, turning 'krud' into 'krund'. It takes Atmanepada endings in its natural form to describe someone submerging. When used with a causative affix (nic), it takes Parasmaipada/Ubhayapada endings to describe immersing or dipping an object into liquid.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana (regular Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The fish plunges into the water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic pratyaya (causative), kartari prayoga, lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to sink or submerges something
scenarios.example_english: The boy submerges the vessel in water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: krudi nimajjane. idid ayam. idito num dhatoh iti num. krundate. cukrunde. krundita. krundishyate. akrundishta.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: krudi nimajjane. iditvat num. krundate. caturvargadipika-prayogeshu nimajjanarthe krundadishu dharana-kriya drishyate.

meanings.English: to sink, to plunge, to submerge, to immerse

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'mud' means to be happy, to rejoice, or to feel joy. In its basic Atmanepada form (modate), the subject naturally feels or experiences happiness inside. When used in the causative form with the 'nic' suffix (modayati), it means to make someone else happy or to delight others.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari Prayoga (Basic Present Tense, Atmanepada)
scenarios.example_english: The child rejoices with his friend.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative, Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The beautiful forest delights everyone.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'muda~ harshe' is marked with anudatta-it, making it inherently Atmanepadi. By application of Guna to the medial vowel 'u', the form 'modate' is derived in Sarvadhatuka environments. Words like 'moda', 'pramoda', and 'modaka' (delighting, sweetmeat) are derived directly from this base.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines 'mud' in the core semantic domain of internal joy (harsha). It takes the standard set augment 'it' in Ardhadhatuka tenses and moods, producing forms like 'mumude' (perfect) and 'amodishta' (aorist).

meanings.English: to rejoice, to be happy, to delight
meanings.Hindi: harshit hona, prasanna hona, anandit hona

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣud' denotes the action of crushing, pounding, or grinding something into small particles. In the basic present tense, it takes Ātmanepada endings (e.g., kṣodate), showing that the subject performs the act of pulverizing or trampling an object.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer grinds/pounds the grain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: He/She causes something to be crushed/ground.
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the cook to crush the herb.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: kṣuda~ saṃpeṣaṇe. anudāttettvād ātmanepadam. aniṭ. kṣodate, cukṣude, kṣottā, kṣotsyate, akṣutta. saṃpeṣaṇaṃ cūrṇībhāvaparyantam mardanam.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: kṣuda~ saṃpeṣaṇe. kṣodate, cukṣude. saṃpeṣaṇaṃ cūrṇīkaraṇam.

meanings.English: to pound, to grind, to pulverize, to crush

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klind' (aupadeshika: klidi) means to become very wet, moist, or to soften and decay due to excess moisture. Because it has an 'i' as an indicator (idit), it takes a nasal (n) insertion before the final consonant, forming 'klindate'. In its causative (nic) form, it expresses making something wet or damp.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), Atmanepada, Prathama-purusha, Eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: Becomes wet or decays from moisture
scenarios.example_english: The garment gets soaked with water due to the rain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat-lakara, Parasmaipada
scenarios.example_english: Water moistens the clay.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: klidi pariklede. Idittvat num. Klindate. Parikledo nama adribhavanam, snehah, kledanam va. Asya dravibhava eva arthah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: klidi pariklede. Idit. Klindate. Parikledo 'rdribhavah. Kledanam nama jalasamparkat ardrabhavah.

meanings.English: To become wet, moist, or soften with moisture

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vardh' means 'to grow', 'to increase', or 'to thrive'. In its basic Atmanepada form (vardhate), it describes something growing or developing naturally on its own. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it shifts to Parasmaipada (vardhayati) and means 'to cause to grow', 'to foster', or 'to nurture'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Atmanepada, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The tree grows with water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, Parasmaipada, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wise person increases knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti classifies 'vardha vriddhau' as an Atmanepadi root of the Bhvadi class. Being anudattopadesha-adjacent and set, it takes the intermediate 'i' augment (it) in non-sarvadhatuka forms, yielding forms like vardhate, vavardhe, vardhita, and vardhishyate.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin comments on 'vardha vriddhau' by equating vriddhi with upacaya (expansion, augmentation, or development). He establishes that it is inherently intransitive in its primary state, operating smoothly with upasargas to denote specialized growth or expansion.

meanings.English: to grow, to increase, to thrive, to prosper

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The verb root svad means to taste, relish, or make food pleasant and sweet. In its standard form, it takes Atmanepada endings (svadate) to describe experiencing or relishing a good flavor. When used in causative (Nic), it signifies making something savory, sweetening, or feeding tasty food to someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The boy relishes the sweet fruit.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic-pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara
scenarios.example_english: The mother sweetens the pudding with sugar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: svada asvadane. anudattetvad atmanepadam. asvadanam nama rasasya anubhavah rucyutpadanam ca. svadate, sasvade, svadita, asvadista.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: svada asvadane. atmanepadi set. asvadanam rasendriyena rucikaranam grahanam ca. svadate.

meanings.English: to taste, to relish, to sweeten, to be pleasant to the palate
meanings.Bengali: svad loa, asvadan kara, misti kara
meanings.Russian: probovat na vkus, naslazhdatsya vkusom, uslazhdat

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dad' belongs to the 1st conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and strictly uses Atmanepada verb terminations to mean 'to give' or 'to bestow'. When the causative suffix (nic) is added, it means 'to cause someone to give'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.example_english: The compassionate person gives food to the needy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha (third person), Ekavacana (singular)
scenarios.meaning: causes to give / makes someone donate
scenarios.example_english: The mother causes the child to give fruit to the beggar.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'dada' is listed in the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'dane' (giving). Being anudatta-it, it operates strictly in the Atmanepada. Conjugation takes standard 'sap' vikarana yielding forms such as dadate, dadate, dadante in present tense, and adadista in the aorist (lun).
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin categorizes 'dada' as a distinct 1st-gana root denoting charity or offering ('dane'). It is seṭ and distinct from the juhotyadi class root 'dan' (da/dadati), retaining its unreduplicated base followed by sap.

meanings.English: To give, to bestow, to donate, to present

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vandh' (aupadeshika 'vandhi') belongs to the first conjugation group (Bhvadi) and means 'to bind', 'to tie', or 'to restrain'. Because it is an Atmanepada verb, it takes middle endings such as -te, -ete, -nte. In sentences, it describes the act of binding or tying objects or animals.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Prathama-purusha (3rd person), Ekavacana (singular), Lat-lakara (present tense)
scenarios.example_english: The cowherd binds the cow with a rope.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Prathama-purusha (3rd person), Bahuvacana (plural), Lan-lakara (imperfect past tense)
scenarios.example_english: The brothers tied the logs together.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'vadi' (or 'vandhi') is listed in the Bhvadi class in the sense of 'bandhana' (tying/binding). Because of its idit character, it takes a penultimate nasal (num-agama), resulting in the base 'vandh-'. Being marked with an anudatta vowel as an it, it exclusively takes Atmanepada affixes, yielding standard present forms like vandhate, vandhete, vandhante.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin comments under the Bhvadi section that this root denotes restriction or binding ('bandhane'). The presence of the marker 'i' necessitates the nasal insertion, and the root inflects regularly as an Atmanepada set-dhatu, forming vandhate, vavandhe, vandhita, and vandhisyate.

meanings.English: To bind, to tie, to fasten, to restrain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'klath' denotes causing harm, injuring, or hurting someone. Because it is an Atmanepadi root, its basic present-tense form ends with '-te' (klathate). When used in the causative form with the affix 'nic', it changes to Parasmaipada (klathayati), meaning to cause someone to injure or destroy an enemy.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The fierce enemy injures the soldier.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Nic pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.meaning: causes to harm / causes to strike down
scenarios.example_english: The king causes the evil-doers to be struck down through the general.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: klatha himsayayam. anudattettvad atmanepadi. klathate, caklathe, klathita, klathishyate. himsa prananiyojanam pidanam va.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: klatha himsayayam. anudattet. klathate. himsa vadharupa pidadirupa ca.

meanings.English: to injure, to hurt, to kill
meanings.Bengali: himsa kara, aghat kara, badh kara

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pan' means 'to praise', 'to admire', or 'to commend'. In the present tense, it optionally takes the suffix '-aya-' by rule (forming 'panayate') or conjugates directly as 'panate'. Because it is conjugated in the Atmanepada, the action reflects an internal feeling of admiration or honoring of someone or something.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (Lat lakara), prathama-purusha, ekavacana with 'aya' pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The virtuous person praises the meritorious one.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Present tense (Lat lakara), prathama-purusha, ekavacana without 'aya' pratyaya
scenarios.example_english: The student honors the teacher.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'pana' belongs to Bhvadi-gana and is taught in the sense of praise ('stutau'). By the rule 'gupadhupavicipanipanibhya ayaḥ', it takes the affix 'aya' in sarvadhatuka contexts, yielding 'panayate', while in ardhadhatuka contexts, 'aya' is optional.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes that 'pana stutau' denotes laudation and respectful admiration. It aligns in meaning with 'pan vyavahare stutau ca' but here is specified essentially for praise.

meanings.English: to praise, to commend, to admire

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bham' means to become angry or rage. It is an Atmanepada verb, taking endings like -te, -ete, -nte. When someone gets angry, the standard form 'bhamate' is used. In causative (nic), it changes to 'bhamayati' meaning 'to make someone angry or provoke'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Out of fury, the enemy rages.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The wicked person's words enrage the sage.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: bhama krodhe. anudatteta atmanepadi. bhamate. babhame. bhamita / bhanta. krodharthatvad akarmakah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: bhama krodhe. bhamate. krodhah amarshah.

meanings.English: to be angry, to rage

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root krath means to hurt, injure, or kill. In standard active voice (Parasmaipada), it indicates someone directly harming an enemy or obstacle. When adding the causative suffix (Nic), it changes to krathayati, meaning causing someone or something to be harmed or destroyed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Active Voice, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The brave warrior strikes down the enemy in battle.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative form, Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana)
scenarios.meaning: Causes to be killed or destroyed
scenarios.example_english: The king gets the wicked individuals subdued through the soldiers.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies the root kratha in the sense of himsayam (violence, hurting, killing). As an unaccented vowel-ending indicator, it belongs to the Bhvadi class taking Parasmaipada endings, forming krathati in the present tense and cakratha in the perfect tense without vocalic lengthening in simple forms.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes kratha himsayam as a transitive root signifying injury and torment. The grammatical derivations proceed regularly with standard guna and intermediate 'i' augment (it) where applicable in ardhadhatuka environments, yielding forms like krathitah.

meanings.English: To kill, injure, hurt, or destroy

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'man' belongs to the Bhvadi class and means 'to praise', 'to honor', or 'to respect'. In its basic form, it takes Atmanepada endings ('manate') when someone praises or honors someone. When used with a causative suffix (Nic), it changes to 'manayati', meaning 'to cause someone to praise' or 'to celebrate/commemorate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Bhvadi Gana, Lat Lakara, Kartari Prayoga (Active Voice, Atmanepada), Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The devotee praises Lord Hari.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic Pratyaya (Causative), Lat Lakara, Prathama Purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The people celebrate the festival.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'mana stutau' under the Bhvadi class as an anudattet root, thereby yielding purely Atmanepada inflectional forms (manate, mamne, manita). It denotes the semantic action of praising or singing eulogies.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin in Kshiratarangini notes that 'mana' is assigned the meaning of 'stuti' (eulogy, glorification). In conjunction with regular Bhvadi derivation, it takes the standard Shap vikarana with intermediate 'i' in non-sarvadhatuka affixes.

meanings.English: to praise, to honor, to respect

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhyai' means to meditate, reflect, or contemplate deeply upon an object or thought. In simple active voice (Parasmaipada), the agent performs the meditation directly. When used with causative affixes, it indicates prompting or guiding another person to focus and meditate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present active indicative (lat, kartari prayoga, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: He or she meditates or contemplates
scenarios.example_english: The sage meditates upon God in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative present indicative (nic, lat, kartari prayoga, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: He or she causes someone to meditate
scenarios.example_english: The teacher leads the disciple to meditate.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhyai cintayam. The root undergoes atva substitution by the rule adeca upadeseasiti, changing dhyai to dhya in non-sit environments, forming dhyayati in sarvadhatuka and dadhyau, dhyata in ardhadhatuka contexts.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhyai cintayam. Included among the diphthong-ending roots that take the atva replacement. It forms dhyayati with sap affixation and illustrates pure contemplation or deep mental absorption.

meanings.English: to meditate, to contemplate, to reflect upon

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'bhi' (bhinī) means to tremble, shake, or move because of fear. Because it is an Atmanepada root in this gana, its basic forms take Atmanepada endings like '-te' (e.g., bhenate). When someone or something makes another person tremble in fear, the causative affix 'nic' is added, producing causative forms like 'bhinayati' or 'bhayayati'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The deer trembles in fear from the lion.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to tremble in fear / frightens
scenarios.example_english: The tiger makes everyone tremble in fear.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root bhini is given in the sense of bhayacalana (movement or trembling caused by fear). The anubandha 'ni' marks it as an Atmanepada root. In the present tense sarvadhatuka environment, guna of the root vowel 'i' yields 'e', leading to the regular Bhvadi stem formation 'bhena-' and the form 'bhenate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes bhini bhayacalane as an Atmanepadavidhi root belonging to the first gana. It indicates physical shaking or agitation arising specifically out of fright or terror (bhayajanita-kampa).

meanings.English: to tremble with fear, to shake, to be frightened
meanings.Hindi: dar se kampna, bhayabhit hokar hilna

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shi' (aupadeshika: shin) means 'to sleep', 'to recline', or 'to lie down'. Because it has an indicatory 'n' (nit), it is conjugated exclusively in Atmanepada. In the causative (nic), it means 'to put to sleep' or 'to cause someone to lie down'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (present tense / lat lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.example_english: The child sleeps on the bed.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: nic-pratyaya (causative present tense / lat lakara, 3rd person singular)
scenarios.meaning: puts to sleep / causes to lie down
scenarios.example_english: The mother puts the baby to sleep.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'shin' is classified under svapne (in the sense of sleeping or resting). Being anudanet/nit, it takes Atmanepada affixes. Guna vowel modification occurs appropriately in Sarvadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'shin svapne' as referring to the act of lying down or sleeping. The nit marker ensures exclusive Atmanepada endings in primary non-causative conjugations.

meanings.English: to sleep, to recline, to lie down

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shri' primarily means to take shelter, resort to, cling to, or serve. Because it has the marker 'n' (shrin) in Panini's grammar, it takes both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada endings (Ubhayapada). Use Parasmaipada (shrayati) when the action is directed outwards or neutrally, and Atmanepada (shrayate) especially when emphasizing that the refuge or benefit of serving is for oneself.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: resorts to / takes refuge in / serves
scenarios.example_english: The devotee takes refuge in Lord Hari.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada, Lat lakara (present tense), prathama purusha, ekavacana (svarita-n-it)
scenarios.example_english: The student resorts to knowledge (for self-growth).

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'shrin' is placed in the meaning of seva (service, resorting to). It is marked with 'n' (nitvat), which ordains both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada as per 'svaritanitaḥ kartrabhipraye kriyaphale'. Being anudatta in upadesha, it is inherently anit.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin explains 'shrin sevayam' as denoting ashraya (resorting, leaning upon) and upupasana (serving, honoring). In sarvadhatuka affixes, it undergoes guna to produce forms such as shrayati and shrayate.

meanings.English: to serve, to resort to, to take shelter in, to lean upon
meanings.Hindi: ashray lena, seva karna, sharan me jana
meanings.Bengali: ashray neoa, seva kora, chorone sthan neoa
meanings.German: zuflucht nehmen zu, dienen, sich stutzen auf
meanings.French: recourir a, se refugier aupres de, servir

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'yu' means to mix, blend, or unite things together. Because it has an indicatory 'ṅ' (yuṅ) in the Dhatupatha, it strictly takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form, yielding forms like 'yavate'. When made causative, it means causing someone to mix or join components.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga, ātmanepada, laṭ, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The cook mixes honey with milk.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇic-pratyaya (causative), parasmaipada, laṭ, prathama-puruṣa, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The physician makes the student mix the medicine.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: yuṅ miœraṇe. Ātmanepadī, aniṭ. miœraṇaṃ sambhandha-karaṇam. yavate, yuvāte, yuvante. Œarvadhātuke guṇaḥ, av-ādeœaḥ.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: yuṅ miœraṇe. ṅitvād ātmanepadam. yavate, yuvate. aniṭkārikāsu yu-dhātu-pāṭhaḥ.

meanings.English: to mix, to blend, to unite

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dru' (marked as druṅ in this entry) means to run, move swiftly, or dissolve/melt. Because of the marker letter 'ṅ', it takes Ātmanepada endings in its direct primary forms. When converted into a causative (making someone run), it uses the ṇic suffix.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Laṭ lakāra, Prathama puruṣa, Ekavacana (Ātmanepada via ṅit marker)
scenarios.example_english: The deer runs quickly in the forest.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (ṇic pratyaya), Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada
scenarios.meaning: causes to run / chases away / melts
scenarios.example_english: The hunter causes the deer to flee with an arrow.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'druṅ' is placed in the Bhvādi gaṇa in the sense of motion (gatau). The anubandha 'ṅ' indicates that the verb takes Ātmanepada terminations under the rule 'anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam'. Being an u-kārānta root, it undergoes guṇa ('o') before śap, followed by av-ādeśa yielding 'dravate'. In Liṭ it forms 'dudruve', and in Luṅ it forms 'adroṣṭa'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin classifies 'druṅ' as an ātmanepadī gatyartha root. The derivation follows standard Bhvādi sarvadhātuka guṇa rules, taking forms such as dravate, dudruve, drotā, droṣyate. It is an aniṭ root.

meanings.English: to run, to move swiftly, to flow, to melt
meanings.French: courir, se déplacer rapidement, couler, fondre

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṣu' carries an indicatory 'ṅ' (kṣuṅ), which mandates Ātmanepada terminations under the rule 'anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam'. It denotes producing a sound, vocalizing, or rustling. In the causative form, adding the suffix 'ṇic' shifts the meaning to causing someone or something to make a sound.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat-lakāra (present indicative), Prathama-puruṣa (third person), Ekavacana (singular) with Ātmanepada
scenarios.example_english: The leaf rustles (makes a sound) due to the effect of the wind.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ṇic-pratyaya), Parasmaipada, Lat-lakāra, Prathama-puruṣa, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: Causes to sound / makes something produce a noise
scenarios.example_english: The boy causes the bell to make a sound.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṣuṅ' belongs to the Bhvādi-gaṇa and is categorized under 'śabde' (in the sense of producing sound). The anubandha 'ṅ' assigns it strictly to the Ātmanepada category. Under the influence of standard guṇa and 'av' substitution before the Śap pratyaya, it conjugates as kṣavate in the present tense and cukṣuve in the perfect tense.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshiraswamin identifies 'kṣuṅ śabde' as an Ātmanepada aniṭ root. He observes that vocalization and sound production are the primary semantic properties, resulting in forms such as kṣavate and cukṣāte.

meanings.English: To make a sound, to rustle, to produce noise
meanings.Hindi: Dhvani karna, aavaz nikalna, shabd karna
meanings.French: Faire un bruit, emettre un son

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'sru' means to flow, trickle, or stream. In its basic form (Parasmaipada), it describes liquids moving naturally, like water from a spring or river. When used with a causative affix (Nic), it changes to mean 'to make flow' or 'to pour/shed'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara (present tense), 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: Water flows from the mountain.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (causative), Lat lakara, 3rd person singular
scenarios.example_english: The child sheds tears.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'srun gatau' belongs to the Bhvadi class. Being 'anit' and ending in 'u', it takes guna 'o' in the sarvadhatuka environment, which becomes 'av' before vowel-initial affixes (forming sravati, asravat, sravet). In the perfect tense (lit), reduplication gives 'susrava'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'sru gatau' implies continuous linear movement or oozing of fluids. The root takes the standard Bhvadi vikarana 'shap' (a), generating regular Parasmaipada forms without an it-agama in anit environments.

meanings.English: to flow, trickle, stream, ooze

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cyu' means to move, trickle, slip, or deviate from a place. Because it has an indicatory 'ṅ' (cyuṅ), it exclusively takes Atmanepada endings in basic usage (cyavate). When made causative with Nic (cyavayati/cyavayate), it means to cause someone or something to move, fall, or deviate.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.meaning: moves, trickles, slips, or falls away
scenarios.example_english: The fruit falls from the tree.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to move, shakes, or causes to fall
scenarios.example_english: The wind causes the leaf to fall.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Cyuṅ gatau - ṅit-tvād ātmanepadī. Cyavate, cucyuve, cyotā, cyoṣyate. Gati-visheṣe sravaṇe calane ca asya prayogo dṛśśate. Aniṭ-kāryaṃ bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Cyuṅ gatau - cyavate. Cyutiḥ ityata eva. Gatau calane ca vartate, anit.

meanings.English: to move, to fall from, to trickle, to deviate
meanings.Bengali: chola, jhora, bhrashto howa, poton howa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'plu' expresses motion involving floating, swimming, or leaping. Because it has an anubandha marker 'ṅ' (pluṅ), it operates primarily in the Ātmanepada voice (e.g., plavate). When used with a causative affix (ṇic), it shifts to Parasmaipada (plāvayati), expressing the act of making something float, inundating, or washing over.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Base root with standard Kartari (active) present tense Ātmanepada affix (śap + te)
scenarios.example_english: A piece of wood floats on water.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative affix (ṇic) + Parasmaipada present affix (ti)
scenarios.meaning: causes to float, submerges, or inundates
scenarios.example_english: The flow of water inundates the village.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti identifies 'pluṅ gatau' as an Ātmanepada root due to its ṅit marker. It undergoes guṇa to 'o' before śap, becoming 'av' via sandhi to derive the present tense form 'plavate'. In perfect tense (liṭ), reduplication yields 'pupluve'. It signifies specific movements such as leaping, swimming, floating, and submerging.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'pluṅ' as indicating a special gait or motion (pluti/gati-viśeṣa), such as jumping like a frog or bird, or moving effortlessly over the surface of water.

meanings.English: to float, to swim, to leap, to jump
meanings.Hindi: tairana, kudana, tairate hue aage badhana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'pra' (aupadeshika 'praṇ') expresses the action of filling, completing, or satisfying. In standard active usage (Parasmaipada), it describes an agent filling a container or satisfying a desire. When used with causative affixes, it conveys causing something to become completely filled or fulfilled.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (active voice), Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: Water fills the pot.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (causative), Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, prathama-purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The seeker causes the bowl to be filled with water.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'praṇ pūraṇe' is listed in the Bhvadi-gana with a terminal nakara as an it-marker. It denotes the act of filling or satiating (pūranam). It is sakarmaka (transitive) and anit in standard siddhi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'praṇ pūraṇe' as conveying the sense of completely filling up a space or satiation (paripūrnatva). Forms in derived and causative conjugations regularly show a-kara lengthening and yuk-agama.

meanings.English: to fill, to satisfy, to make full

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shru' fundamentally means to hear or to listen. In its primary active form, it undergoes a special Paninian rule ('shruvah shri cha') taking the 'snu' affix to form 'shrinoti' (he/she hears). When converted into the causative form using the Nich affix, it becomes 'shravayati' (he/she causes someone to hear, tells, or recites).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara, with snu-vikarana and shri replacement
scenarios.example_english: The student listens to the teacher's words.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nich pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara
scenarios.meaning: causes to hear, narrates, or recites
scenarios.example_english: The mother narrates a story to the child.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: Sayana details that 'shru shravane' takes the snu vikarana and root-stem substitution 'shri' via the sutra 'shruvah shri cha' (3.1.74) in sarvadhatuka affixes, yielding 'shrinoti'. It is anit in primary formations and forms 'shushrava' in Lit and 'ashrausheet' in Lun with vriddhi.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin analyzes 'shravana' as auditory cognition (shabda-grahana). He highlights the root's anit nature, its regular guna/vriddhi shifts in ardhadhatuka contexts, and regular causative derivations like 'shravayati'.

meanings.English: to hear, to listen

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'vṛ' with the silent marker 'ṅ' expresses serving, honoring, or devotedly choosing someone. Because of the 'ṅ' marker, it takes Ātmanepada endings such as -te, -ete, and -ante, producing the present tense form 'varate'.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga (Ātmanepada, Lat Lakāra, Prathama Puruṣa, Ekavacana)
scenarios.example_english: The student always serves and honors the teacher.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Causative (Ņic pratyaya, Ātmanepada, Lat Lakāra)
scenarios.meaning: causes someone to choose or formally solicits
scenarios.example_english: The king appoints (chooses) the scholar to the position of minister.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The entry explains 'vṛṅ sambhaktau' as a root in the Bhvādi-gaṇa marked with ṅit for Ātmanepada. 'Sambhakti' designates sevana (devoted service) or vibhajana (sharing/participation). It undergoes regular guṇa before the sārvadhātuka affix śap to form 'varate'.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kṣīrasvāmin glosses 'sambhakti' as loving service, worship, and faithful selection. The vowel undergoes guṇa yielding 'varate', and in the perfect tense (liṭ) forms 'vavre'.

meanings.English: to serve, to honor, to choose devotedly, to share
meanings.Bengali: seba kara, barana kara, bhajana kara
meanings.Chinese: shi feng, jing feng, xuan ze

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'dhri' belongs to the first group of verbs and specifically means to remain, endure, stay firm, or stay alive. Because of the marker letter 'ṅ' in its original Paninian form (dhriṅ), it strictly takes Atmanepada endings in its basic form (dharate). When a causative affix (Nic) is added, it means to cause to stay, hold, or sustain (dhārayati).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat lakara (Present Tense), Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: He stays firm with courage in times of difficulty.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat lakara, Prathama purusha, Ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The earth supports all living beings.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: dhriṅ avasthane. ṅittvād ātmanepadī. avasthānaṃ sthitiḥ prāṇadhāraṇaṃ ca. dharate, dadhre, dhartā, dhariṣyate iti rūpāṇi bhavanti.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: dhriṅ avasthane. avasthānaṃ sthitau vartate jīvane ca. anit. dharate, dadhre ityādi.

meanings.English: to remain, to stay, to endure, to hold on, to subsist
meanings.Hindi: thaharana, sthir rahana, tikana, jivit rahana

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'kṛp' means 'to be capable' or 'to be fit for'. It is inherently used in the Ātmanepada. When used in simple present tense, it shows someone's ability or fitness for an action. When conjugated in the causative (Nic), it conveys making someone capable or enabling someone.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: kartari prayoga (standard Atmanepada present indicative)
scenarios.meaning: is capable, is fit, has the ability
scenarios.example_english: The boy is capable in the work.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: ṇyanta (causative Parasmaipada)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher makes the student capable in knowledge.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The root 'kṛpū' belongs to Bhvādi-gaṇa and carries the semantic sense of 'sāmarthya' (capability or fitness). Being anudāttet by marker, it takes standard Ātmanepada terminations forming 'kṛpate' in the present tense (laṭ). In unaugmented situations, it retains the ṛ-vowel without standard guṇa in certain non-sarvadhātuka environments unless specified.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes 'kṛpū sāmarthye' denoting internal capacity or adequacy. It is classified under anudāttet roots taking Ātmanepada affixes, deriving regular forms such as 'kṛpate', 'cakṛpe', and 'kṛpitā'.

meanings.English: to be capable, to be able, to be fit

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'gam' means 'to go'. In the present tense, 'gam' changes its stem to 'gacch-' before standard endings, giving forms like 'gacchati' (he/she goes). When we want to express causing someone else to go (causative / nic), the stem changes to 'gamay-', giving 'gamayati' (causes to go / sends).

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (Simple Present)
scenarios.example_english: The boy goes to school.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic-pratyaya (Causative), Lat-lakara
scenarios.example_english: The father causes the son to go to the village.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: gaml gatau. idamudattaudanityah. gacchati, jagama, gantasi, gamisyati. lrit-karah anubandhah 'lrito va' ityasyarthah. gatyarthatvat sakarmakah.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: gaml gatau. 'isugamiyamanam chah' iti chakaratvam. gacchati, jagama, ganta, gamisyati. anit parasmaipadi.

meanings.English: to go, to move, to reach, to attain

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root kram means to step, walk, or make progress. When used in Parasmaipada, the vowel lengthens to form kramati. When prefixed with certain preverbs (upasargas like pra, vi, or ati) or used in specific semantic conditions like beginning an action or showing power, it frequently takes Atmanepada endings without lengthening.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara (rule kramah parasmaipadeshu)
scenarios.example_english: The boy steps along the path.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Atmanepada with upasarga 'pra' indicating commencement
scenarios.meaning: sets forth or begins an endeavor
scenarios.example_english: The student begins to study.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Vritti explains kramu in the sense of pada-vikshepa (stepping or moving feet). It highlights that the anubandha 'u' indicates optional it-agama (udit vat) in Ardhadhatuka forms. It elaborates on the lengthening of the vowel in Parasmaipada by Paninian rule 7.3.76, and details specific Atmanepada allocations under rules 1.3.38 to 1.3.43 governed by prefixes and contextual nuances.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin defines the root as pacing or striding. He discusses the lengthening in Parasmaipada (kramatiti dirghah) versus the short base retention in Atmanepada (kramate). He also traces primary nominal derivatives including kramah (order/sequence), vikramah (valor/stepping out), and parakramah (prowess).

meanings.English: to step, to stride, to walk, to progress

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'khan' means to dig or tear open the ground. In Parasmaipada (khanati), the action of digging is stated generally. In Atmanepada (khanate), it emphasizes that the fruit of digging belongs to the subject. In the causative form (khanayati), someone gets a well or pit dug by laborers.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The farmer digs a pit in the field.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Nic pratyaya (Causative), Parasmaipada, Lat lakara, prathama purusha, ekavacana
scenarios.example_english: The king gets a well dug in the village.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: khanu avadarane. avadaranam bhumividaranam. ukaro 'nudattettvaprayojanah, tena svaritetvat ubhayapaditvam sidhyati. anit ayam dhatu.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: khanu avadarane. avadaranam bhumer bhindanam. khanati, khanate. nisthayam khatah iti bhavatah.

meanings.English: to dig, excavate, tear open

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'shas' belongs to the first conjugation (Bhvadi gana) and takes Parasmaipada endings. It means to instruct, discipline, teach, or govern. When a subject guides or issues instructions to an object, this root takes regular thematic conjugational markers (a-pratyaya) yielding forms like shasati.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lat-lakara (present tense), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The teacher instructs the student.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Kartari prayoga, Lan-lakara (past imperfect), prathama-purusha, eka-vacana
scenarios.example_english: The king governed the citizens righteously.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: The Madhaviya Dhatuvritti analyzes 'shasu anushistau' as an instruction and governance-denoting root of the Bhvadi class. It undergoes the standard Shap vikarana in sarvadhatuka affixes, forming shasati, shasatah, shasanti in the present tense, taking intermediate i (it) in ardhadhatuka environments.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: Kshirasvamin notes under Kshiratarangini that the verbal root 'shasu' has the primary sense of 'anushisti' (systematic moral or intellectual instruction, or regulation). It is treated as parasmaipadi and set in derivation, yielding regular thematic forms distinct from the reduplicating Adadi root shas.

meanings.English: to instruct, teach, govern, discipline
meanings.Hindi: anushasan karna, upadesh dena, shasan karna
meanings.Bengali: upadesh dewa, shashon kora, shikkha dewa

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root 'cakṣ' means to articulate speech clearly or to describe/perceive distinctly. Because of the ending 'ṅ' marker (anubandha), it is inherently conjugated in the Ātmanepada voice. In common Sanskrit usage, especially with prefixes, it expresses narration, clear speech, or observing and telling.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Simple present tense (laṭ, prathama-puruṣa, ekavacana, kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The teacher explains the truth clearly.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Prefix 'ā' + simple present tense (laṭ, kartari prayoga)
scenarios.example_english: The sage narrates the story of the Ramayana.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: cakṣiṅ vyaktāyāṃ vāci. 'ṅ' itkaraṇaḥ ātmanepadārthaḥ. asya ārdhadhātuke 'cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ' iti khyāñ-ādeśo bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: cakṣiṅ vyaktāyāṃ vāci. vyaktoktāvityarthaḥ. caṣṭe, cakṣāte, cakṣate. ārdhadhātukaviṣaye asya khyāñ-ādeśaḥ prayujyate.

meanings.English: to speak clearly, to tell, to articulate, to observe

dhaturupanandini.simple_explanation: The root yaj means to worship gods, to bring people together or associate, and to give in charity. Because it has a special svarita marker, it can take both Parasmaipada and Atmanepada endings depending on who receives the spiritual fruit of the sacrifice.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Parasmaipada (kartrabhipraye kriyaphale asati - fruit goes to another)
scenarios.meaning: Worships or conducts a sacrifice on behalf of someone else
scenarios.example_english: The priest performs the sacrifice for the benefit of the king.

scenarios.grammar_trigger: Atmanepada (kartrabhipraye kriyaphale sati - fruit goes to oneself)
scenarios.meaning: Sacrifices or worships for one's own spiritual benefit
scenarios.example_english: The patron performs the sacrifice for his own attainment of heaven.

vritti_extracts.madhaviya_dhatuvritti: yaja devapujasangatikaranadaneshu. devapujanam arcanam, sangatikaranam melanam, danam svatvanivrttipurvakam parasvatvapadanam. svaritetvat kartrabhipraye phale atmanepadam, anyatha parasmaipadam bhavati.
vritti_extracts.kshiratarangini: yaja devapujadisvarthah. svaritet. yajati, yajate. samprasarana-vidhau grahijyavayi-vyadhibrascabhrasjabhurjasuncinam ityadina samprasaranam iyaja ije ityadau.

meanings.English: to worship, to sacrifice, to unite, to give
